title: Oil dips as Trump waives Russia energy sanctions, offsetting Hormuz tanker blast
body: The early dip is modest, which suggests traders see the Russia waiver as a supply cushion rather than a game-changer while Hormuz risk remains live. Diesel is the product to watch: any sign that Russian product exports are rising would ease pressure on middle distillate cracks, which have carried much of the tightness from refinery attacks. Against that, a confirmed mine strike in Hormuz would revive the shipping-risk premium quickly, and war-risk insurance and freight costs could rise further. A Pakistani diplomatic visit to Tehran offers a faint de-escalation thread, but the market is likely to treat it cautiously until there is substance. Expect headline-driven, two-way trade. --- Earlier: Euro slides against Australian dollar as three European headwinds hit early trade --- Trump has chosen to keep Russian barrels flowing to keep Moscow talking, and for now that is enough to outweigh the latest flash point in the Strait of Hormuz.

title: New Zealand trade deficit widens to nearly NZ$2 billion, more than double forecasts
body: A wider trade gap is a modest negative for the New Zealand dollar at the margin, since a larger external deficit means more reliance on foreign funding. Oil is the key channel to watch: with the Iran war keeping crude prices elevated, any confirmation that fuel drove the import jump would point to imported inflation pressure the RBNZ cannot ignore. That cuts against the dovish read from soft domestic demand and keeps further tightening on the table. Rate markets will weigh this against the pause they have leaned toward for 28 October. China's growth data later today matters more for the kiwi's near-term direction, given China's role as a key export market. --- New Zealand is buying more from the world while selling no more to it, and with fuel costs elevated, that imbalance lands squarely on the RBNZ's desk ahead of a pre-election rate call. title: China data preview: industry holds up, consumers and property lag ahead of Q3 GDP
body: For oil, China's position as the largest crude importer makes this release a demand signal at a sensitive moment, with the Iran war already squeezing Gulf supply. Soft domestic numbers would temper the demand side of the oil story even as supply risk keeps prices elevated. The Australian and New Zealand dollars, as proxies for Chinese growth, are exposed to any downside surprise, and the Australian dollar's early gains against the euro could be tested. A weak print would also lift expectations for policy easing, putting Tuesday's loan prime rate decision and the yuan in focus. An upside surprise driven mainly by exports would do little to ease concerns about trade friction. --- More data due today: Economic and event calendar in Asia - China data the focus --- China's export machine is running hot, but with consumers cautious, property still sinking and oil costs climbing, it is not enough to lift growth back to Beijing's target.

title: Oil Slips After Sharp Weekly Rise
body: Crude oil prices slipped to around $101 per barrel on Monday but held on to most of last week's 10% rally, as mounting tensions in the Middle East and Eastern Europe kept supply risks elevated. Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthi rebels showed little sign of easing, with a Saudi helicopter crashing near the Yemeni border and the Houthis targeting Yanbu, a key oil export hub. Over the weekend, three tankers were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran's IRGC navy insisted the waterway remained closed and that vessels could transit only with its authorization. In Europe, Ukrainian strikes triggered fires at an oil export terminal and a storage facility in St. Petersburg on Sunday, after Kyiv launched more than 1,000 drones at Russia in one of the war's largest aerial assaults. Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump announced he had reached a diesel export agreement with Russia and delayed additional sanctions in order to avoid jeopardizing peace negotiations with Ukraine. title: NZX 50 Extends Losses to Start the Week
body: The NZX 50 slipped 44 points, or 0.3%, to 13,710 in Monday morning trading, extending the previous session's losses and hitting its lowest level since October 8. The index followed Friday's decline on Wall Street, driven by ongoing selling in technology stocks. Investor sentiment was cautious ahead of the release of Q3 inflation data and a raft of key Chinese indicators due this week, including GDP growth figures. Risk appetite was further dampened by fresh data showing New Zealand's trade deficit widened sharply in September, as imports grew faster than exports. The downside was partially limited by private-sector data for September, which showed overall activity at a three-month high, with manufacturing growth accelerating and the services sector continuing to expand. Financials, technology, real estate, and energy stocks were the main drags on the index, with notable declines in Mainfreight (-3.0%), Henderson Far East Income (-1.8%), Infratil (-1.6%), Gentrack Group (-1.5%), Channel Infrastructure (-0.9%), and F&C Investment (-0.8%).
